items.title: Govt reaches out to JI, invites party to another round of talks to break deadlock
items.description: LAHORE: Federal Minister for Planning Ahsan Iqbal on Friday contacted Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) Vice Emir Liaqat Baloch and invited the party to another round of talks over its demand for the abolition of the petroleum levy. The government’s renewed contact came as JI Emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman finalised preparations for the party’s Sept 20 march on Islamabad against the levy. According to the JI, Iqbal invited the JI committee, led by Baloch, to talks on Saturday. Baloch said he would respond to the invitation after consulting the party chief and senior leadership. He, however, made it clear that the JI’s protest movement would continue until the petroleum levy was abolished. The latest contact came after several rounds of talks between the government and the JI. The government delegation had initially travelled to Mansoora in Lahore to invite the JI for negotiations, while four subsequent rounds were held in Islamabad. The last round took place on Wednesday, Sept 16. JI claims its proposals can save trillions JI chief Rehman on Friday said the party’s protest movement aimed to press the government for immediate economic relief, asserting that the national exchequer could save between Rs3 trillion and Rs4 trillion if the authorities adopted the party’s proposed fiscal reforms. Addressing a press conference in Islamabad, the JI chief voiced sharp criticism of rising fuel costs and heavy taxation, as well as what he characterised as superficial relief packages that failed to address the core burdens facing the public. Rehman announced that a nationwide “super long march” towards the federal capital would commence on September 20. He rejected the government’s argument that recent energy and fuel price hikes were strictly attributable to international market forces, saying the authorities were relying on aggressive levies to meet revenue targets rather than reducing state expenditure. The JI chief noted that local fuel prices had risen significantly faster than those in neighbouring countries during recent regional tensions, disproportionately affecting lower- and middle-income households that rely heavily on smaller vehicles. Calling for an end to guaranteed profit margins for oil marketing companies at the expense of consumers, Rehman reiterated the JI’s demands to abolish the petroleum levy, end non-productive capacity payments to independent power producers (IPPs) and regasification plants, and fix the price of petrol at Rs225 per litre. Outlining key economic measures, the JI emir called for an immediate cut of three percentage points in the benchmark interest rate, pointing out that every one-percentage-point reduction would save the exchequer approximately Rs574 billion. He said the government must stop protecting commercial bank profits and instead work towards systematically eliminating interest from the national economy. “The public’s support for the party’s movement is growing,” Rehman said, confirming ongoing dialogue and mutual political support with farmers’ alliances and PTI over their respective demonstrations. “The September 20 demonstration will involve caravans travelling to Islamabad from across Sindh, Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, including a dedicated contingent travelling by train from Karachi,” he said. Rehman assured the public that the self-funded march would not involve road blockades or cause unnecessary disruption to daily life, adding that its arrangements would not obstruct students appearing for the upcoming Medical and Dental College Admission Test (MDCAT). While expressing readiness for immediate talks if the government presented actionable proposals, the JI leadership warned that stalling tactics would not be tolerated as public mobilisation intensified.

items.title: US troop deaths during Iran war exceed Pentagon count by at least four, Washington Post reports
items.description: Sept 18 (Reuters) - More US troops have died during the US-Israeli war with Iran than the Pentagon has publicly disclosed, the Washington Post reported on Friday. Defense Secretary PeteHegseth denied the report. The Post, citing five unidentified officials, reported that there had been at least 22 military fatalities, four more than were listed in the data available on the Pentagon's public database.

items.title: Idris appointment freeze worries Juba signatories, drones hit Damazin and North Kordofan prepares for decisive battles, violence erupts in Abyei, Sudan returns to IGAD, but is all rosy?
items.description: Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . Sudan was back at the Intergovernmental Authority on Development’s high-level meetings on Tuesday after nearly two years of frosty relations over the regional bloc’s wartime diplomacy. Khartoum wants to put that tension behind it and take up normal affairs with its neighbors. But with the country still at war and fragmented, IGAD faces a delicate balancing act — keeping Sudan engaged in a regional system in which its instability has reverberating consequences, while navigating Khartoum’s red lines on sovereignty and foreign interference. The Sudanese delegation came pushing its political internal dialogue that Khartoum says should shape what comes next, with no room for regional platforms to impose arrangements from outside. That puts IGAD’s role in Sudan under close scrutiny in Khartoum. The bloc is part of the Quintet mediation mechanism that has been working on a political track outside Sudan. The dialogue Khartoum is rushing forward is aimed at reshaping the political order on its terms ahead of any possible settlement of the war. And that reordering is already unsettling the military’s main political allies — the armed movements signatories to the Juba agreement. A decree by Prime Minister Kamel Idris last week has added to those worries. He froze hiring across the executive branch and ordered preparations for a review of appointments made in recent months, prompting fears among the movements that the power-sharing arrangements created by the Juba peace deal could be gradually changed. Sources close to Idris say the move is intended to prevent new centers of influence from becoming entrenched, and also to rein in spending as Sudan faces an unprecedented economic crisis. A late-August central bank policy change giving banks greater freedom to manage foreign currency was followed by a historic fall in the pound, with the dollar climbing from about 6,400 pounds at the end of August to as much as 8,850 by mid-September. On the battlefield, the military has made its largest push in North Kordofan since July, capturing 11 Rapid Support Forces positions this week and reducing the paramilitary group’s presence to two main positions in the state. Military sources say the battle for North Kordofan is now entering its decisive phase. Farther west, heavy fighting broke out in RSF-held northern Abyei, the disputed territory bordering South Sudan, between the Ngok Dinka and Messiria tribes. Tribal sources said the clashes followed the killing of a member of one of the groups and left casualties in the dozens. In Blue Nile, where the RSF and its allies are pressing toward the state capital, Damazin came under RSF drone attacks on Sunday that killed five civilians and injured others. *** Sudan attends first high-level IGAD meeting after return to regional bloc Foreign Ministry Undersecretary Muawiya Osman Khaled at the 74th extraordinary session of IGAD’s Council of Ministers in Djibouti, September 15. Photo: Sudan’s Foreign Ministry via X. After years of frosty relations born out of disagreements about wartime diplomacy, Sudan officially resumed its participation in IGAD affairs on Tuesday at a foreign ministerial meeting of the governmental bloc. Foreign Ministry Undersecretary Muawiya Osman Khaled led Sudan’s delegation to the 74th extraordinary session of IGAD’s Council of Ministers in Djibouti, alongside Sudan’s ambassador to Djibouti, Mohamed Saeed Hassan. While Sudanese sources told Mada Masr that they have their eyes set on moving past wartime strains to take up normal affairs with their neighbors, the reality of the ongoing war for IGAD officials is that the bloc will have to walk a tightrope, with Khartoum watching closely to see what role IGAD seeks to play in Sudan’s political process and how close it comes to the line the government draws around foreign interference and sovereignty. Tuesday’s meeting marked the latest step in Sudan’s return to the bloc after nearly two years of a self-imposed suspension. The country’s Security and Defense Council approved the return seven months ago, and IGAD reopened its main office in Khartoum in July. At the opening of Tuesday’s meeting, IGAD Executive Secretary Workneh Gebeyehu said Sudan’s return to full participation “restored this family to completeness.” Sudan’s participation in the Tuesday meeting marks “the beginning of a new phase in the relationship with IGAD,” a diplomatic source at the Foreign Ministry told Mada Masr. Khartoum wants to use its return to the bloc to move beyond a relationship defined by the war and mediation efforts and toward cooperation on issues affecting Sudan and its neighbors, including borders, migration, food security and regional trade, the source added. The Sudanese delegation came with a message that the landscape within Sudan has changed. Khaled briefed the ministers on what the government sees as a “significant improvement” in the situation and advances by the armed forces, while also describing the scale of destruction caused by the war and RSF attacks on civilians, according to the source. Khartoum was clear about what it wants that changing landscape to mean politically. The delegation emphasized that the next phase should prioritize the political dialogue it is pushing inside Sudan, rather than allowing regional organizations to become platforms for political arrangements imposed from outside, the source said. The undersecretary called on IGAD to support the internal dialogue, describing it as a process aimed at addressing Sudan’s issues through political and social forces within the country. Khartoum has been working to move that process forward for months. Despite deep disagreements with major political forces over the process itself, the dialogue’s preparatory committee is now working to secure enough participation to get it off the ground. The regional platforms Khartoum said it is seeking to keep from shaping that process have included the Quintet, in which IGAD is a member, alongside the African Union, United Nations, European Union and Arab League. The group has repeatedly brought Sudanese political and civilian stakeholders together in Addis Ababa to develop a roadmap for a political process and form a preparatory committee, with the eventual aim of a transition to civilian-led government. A Quintet delegation visited Khartoum last week, and a member of the dialogue’s preparatory committee told Mada Masr at the time that it met with the committee in the first contact made between the two tracks. For a former IGAD official, Sudan’s return and participation in the ministerial meeting “effectively closes the boycott phase,” but does not erase the disputes of the past two years. The next test, the official said, will be how IGAD handles any role in Sudan’s political processes and coordinates with other initiatives without creating competing tracks. The organization has learned from the past two years that any role it plays in Sudan requires treating the Sudanese government as a central institutional actor while maintaining channels of communication with other Sudanese parties, the former official said. Striking that balance will be essential if IGAD is to regain its position in the Sudan file. That was where the relationship broke down during the war. IGAD was the regional organization most closely involved in Sudan from the outset. But its relationship with Khartoum broke down in 2024, after the government suspended its participation in the bloc over its decision to invite RSF Commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo to extraordinary summits. Khartoum said the invitations “violated national sovereignty,” and viewed them as “unacceptable equivocation between the country’s military institution and a rebel faction, as well as an attempt to grant the RSF international legitimacy at the expense of the Sudanese state,” another Foreign Ministry source previously told Mada Masr. The government also objected to the way IGAD handled its mediation effort and to the involvement of regional actors in the process. The diplomatic source at the Foreign Ministry argued that there is now some common ground. Recent IGAD statements aligned with the government’s position, affirming Sudan’s sovereignty and unity and rejecting parallel governing bodies, the source said. Khartoum now wants to move past the disputes that led to the boycott. But while the two sides are using similar wording to describe a Sudanese-led and Sudanese-owned dialogue, that does not mean they necessarily mean the same thing by it, according to the IGAD former official. They may differ over what that process should entail and which actors should take part, they added. The former official said this is where the two sides could begin to diverge. Khartoum wants the political dialogue to remain inside Sudan and rejects external interference and dictates, and IGAD sees its regional role as including dialogue among Sudanese parties and coordination with international partners. For Khartoum, the diplomatic source stressed, any renewed IGAD role in Sudan must respect the country’s sovereignty and existing institutions. The government wants regional support for its internal dialogue, but not in a form that turns it into an externally imposed negotiating framework. Sudan’s return gives Khartoum more room to make that case inside the organization itself. The source at the IGAD secretariat said its presence now allows the government to engage directly with positions adopted by the bloc and debate them within its institutions. The same question of where to draw the line extends to the humanitarian file. During the meeting, Khaled reaffirmed the government’s commitment to opening border crossings for humanitarian aid, while accusing the RSF of using some aid routes for military supplies and operations, according to the first Foreign Ministry source. The former official said that, too, could become a point of friction with IGAD. The bloc sees Sudan’s humanitarian crisis as having direct regional consequences, while Khartoum insists that aid deliveries must operate under arrangements that preserve state sovereignty. Whatever the tensions, Sudan’s return is important to IGAD as it adjusts to a region that has changed since the war began, the former official said. Red Sea security, borders, migration and food security are now more closely tied to the war, while prolonged instability in Sudan has direct implications for South Sudan, Ethiopia, Chad and Djibouti. The Djibouti meeting was not devoted to Sudan, the source at the IGAD secretariat said. The ministers also discussed a range of regional issues, as well as the organization’s institutional and financial affairs. Ahead of the meeting, the secretariat said the council would discuss regional peace and security, implementation of the IGAD treaty and efforts to strengthen the organization’s institutions. The Djiboutian presidency said its agenda focused primarily on IGAD’s administrative and financial situation and the geopolitical challenges facing the bloc. Sudan came into the discussions on regional peace and security in part because of its geographic position and the war’s effects on neighboring countries, the source said. During his visit, Sudan’s Foreign Ministry undersecretary also delivered a message from Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan to Djiboutian President Ismail Omar Guelleh on bilateral relations and developments in Sudan. A second Sudanese diplomatic source said the message was part of an effort to revive political contacts between Khartoum and Djibouti. Guelleh received the foreign ministers of IGAD member states at the presidential palace after Tuesday’s extraordinary session. The Djiboutian presidency said they discussed the session’s outcome as well as the institutional and geopolitical issues facing the organization. *** Sudanese pound plunges after central bank eases currency controls A policy shift in late August that gave Sudanese banks greater freedom to manage foreign currency has been followed by a historic collapse in the value of the pound. The dollar, which traded at around 6,400 pounds on the parallel market on August 27, reached as much as 8,850 pounds on September 16, according to market traders who spoke to Mada Masr. The move doubled the disparity between bank and parallel-market rates and pushed exchange rate fluctuations directly into the prices of basic goods, imports and other transactions. The Central Bank of Sudan began easing restrictions on banks’ foreign currency operations on August 24, allowing them greater discretion in setting exchange rates and buying export proceeds. The changes were intended to give banks more room to manage the foreign currency available to them. But the added flexibility also gave banks greater scope to acquire foreign currency beyond their immediate needs, adding to demand in the market as the pound came under pressure. The dollar rose steadily through the first half of September, passing 7,000 pounds on September 2 before moving above 8,000 by mid-month. Trading has since become increasingly volatile, with prices varying sharply by location, timing and transaction size and, at times, trading stopping altogether as sellers held back from quoting fixed prices, according to traders. Bank rates in some cases remained around 3,700-4,200 pounds to the dollar while parallel market prices climbed much higher, leaving businesses uncertain about the cost of replacing imported goods and forcing repeated repricing, the traders said. The changes followed earlier restrictions requiring banks to use a central bank-set injection rate for certain import transactions and to coordinate with the central bank before using export proceeds to finance imports. Those requirements were later relaxed. Rather than narrowing the gap between official and parallel market rates, the shift has added another source of demand to a market already short of dollars, contributing to the pound’s rapid decline. But a former senior Finance Ministry official told Mada Masr that the latest fall is rooted in a broader deterioration in the economy rather than a temporary surge in dollar demand or speculation in the parallel market. Foreign currency inflows have weakened, while production and public finances have deteriorated throughout the war, they told Mada Masr. At the same time, demand for foreign currency from importers and individuals trying to protect their savings from erosion has risen. The war has also pushed more transactions into cash and outside the banking system, making it harder for the central bank to influence the money supply and exchange rate. All of this pours into a self-feeding loop in which the falling pound raises the cost of imports and production inputs, which pushes prices higher and, in turn, drives citizens and traders to buy dollars as a hedge, adding new pressure on the exchange rate, according to the former official. Annual inflation reached 45.84 percent in April 2026, according to the Central Bureau of Statistics, while the International Monetary Fund projects average inflation of 75.1 percent for the year. The former official said the central issue is Sudan’s ability to generate stable inflows of foreign currency. The country still has potential sources of dollar income, particularly gold, agriculture, livestock and gum arabic, but the war has disrupted production and export chains and pushed more trade into unofficial channels. Agriculture could provide one of the quickest routes back to higher production, they said, given Sudan’s land, water and existing expertise. But that requires fuel, seeds and other inputs, financing, transport and access to markets, as well as protecting roads and farming areas from the unrest that has disrupted the growing season in many regions. Limited foreign currency should consequently be directed toward inputs that allow production to resume rather than toward imports that can be deferred. They said the government should first move toward a clear exchange-rate policy, gradually narrowing the gap between the official and parallel rates rather than trying to impose an administrative rate divorced from market reality. Multiple rates, they added, encourage speculation and make it harder for businesses to obtain foreign currency through official channels. That does not mean allowing the pound to collapse abruptly. The central bank can intervene when it has the resources to do so, they said, “but it cannot defend an exchange rate unsupported by real resources.” Nor would cracking down on parallel market traders solve the problem. The parallel market exists because official channels are unable to meet much of the demand, they said, and that gap has to be addressed at its source. At the same time, the government needs to bring public spending under control, particularly spending not matched by real output or revenue, the former official said. Financing deficits through monetary expansion adds pressure on prices and the exchange rate, which ties any fix for the pound directly to fiscal reform. The state needs to weigh its spending priorities across core institutions, public services and the war, while curbing unnecessary spending that strains already limited resources, they added. Gold could also provide foreign currency relatively quickly if the sector was further integrated into regulated channels, they said, but it should not become the economy’s only source of dollars. Sudan would need to diversify exports and capture more value from agricultural and livestock products rather than relying mainly on raw resources. The official also pointed to the costs imposed on trade. Multiple fees, along with high transport and procedural costs, make Sudanese exports more expensive and less competitive. Easing movement through ports and border crossings and removing unnecessary charges could increase foreign currency earnings without imposing further restrictions on citizens. The same focus on production, they said, should extend to external aid. Alongside humanitarian support, foreign financing should help restore electricity, transport, irrigation, banking and other infrastructure needed to get production and trade moving again, allowing aid to contribute to the economy’s ability to produce goods and generate foreign currency. The official acknowledged, however, that managing these problems from the center has itself become harder. The war has produced a more fragmented economy, with cash, liquidity and trade moving through different channels in different parts of the country. As a result, authorities have a less complete picture of the money circulating in the economy and of the trade taking place outside formal channels, making monetary policy harder to manage. The former official concluded that any attempt to rebuild Sudan’s economy will have limited impact unless it addresses the relationship between the war, production, public finance and the exchange market all at once. That kind of recovery is the longer road, they said, but it is the only one that can give the currency a real foundation for stability. *** PM’s decision to review hires triggers concerns within armed movements over power-sharing arrangements Prime Minister Kamel Idris and Darfur Governor Minni Arko Minnawi meet in Khartoum, August 31. Photo: Prime Minister Kamel Idris via X. A decision by Prime Minister Kamel Idris to freeze new hires and personnel movements across the executive branch and review appointments made in recent months has raised fears among armed movements signatories to the Juba peace agreement that the review could extend to positions they are entitled to under the peace deal. With no official clarity on the scope of the decision, a senior figure in the Sudan Liberation Movement led by Darfur Governor Minni Arko Minnawi said the concern is that the review could be the start of a gradual process of changing the power-sharing arrangements. The decision, issued on September 8, puts a temporary halt on new appointments, transfers and secondments across government institutions, with exceptions requiring Idris’s prior approval. Institutions must also provide the prime minister’s office with lists of appointments made since May 19 and the reasons for each by September 17. Where staffing gaps exist, the directive calls for employees already in government service who have not been recalled to work to be considered before new appointments are made. A source close to Idris said the measure is meant to bring the government’s staffing structure under control after a period of expanded appointments. The decision is not intended to disrupt the work of state institutions, the source stressed. Rather, it is meant to prevent appointments from continuing on an automatic basis while the government reassesses how employees are distributed across institutions. According to the source, the war has left some institutions with staff who remain away from their workplaces while others have been forced to relocate or are operating with insufficient personnel. The freeze follows a review of government appointments made since Idris took office last year, a source in the prime minister’s office said. A second source close to the premiership said the review of appointments is part of Idris’s effort over the past year to reassess how the executive branch operates. The war has produced overlapping mandates, multiple centers of decision making and an expansion of government structures, the source said. One aim of the review, they added, is to determine whether new positions reflect genuine institutional needs or have created posts that state institutions cannot afford or whose responsibilities they cannot clearly define. The restructuring, the source said, is not limited to appointments. It includes reviewing institutional structures, reducing overlap between government bodies, redistributing employees and keeping decision making within the executive chain of command. The government is also concerned about administrative centers that could become entrenched over time, the source said. Appointments and secondments expanded during the war as institutions tried to keep operating amid displacement and geographic fragmentation. But some of those arrangements risk becoming permanent fixtures as conditions change, making it harder down the line to adjust personnel and administrative structures, with new centers of influence potentially gaining enough sway to obstruct such changes independent of the central executive authority, according to the source. A source close to Burhan described a similar concern from within the TSC chair’s inner circle. The aim, in their view, is to stop wartime arrangements from becoming a fixed arrangement. The armed movements, however, fear the review could extend beyond administrative restructuring to positions created through political settlements, particularly those tied to the Juba agreement. The senior figure in the SLM (Minnawi) said the movement has no objection in principle to reviewing appointments or regulating the civil service. Its concern is that a blanket administrative decision could be used to reshuffle positions that are governed by those arrangements. The source described the decision as a potential “expansion of the use of authority” if applied broadly to institutions covered by the peace agreement. In its current form, the decision does not clearly distinguish between ordinary administrative positions and posts created through political agreements, the source said. “The problem is not reviewing appointments, but giving a single authority the power to determine the fate of all appointments and personnel movements within state institutions without clearly defining the exceptions or which bodies the decision applies to,” the source said. The armed movements entered state institutions under political and constitutional arrangements set out in the Juba agreement, the source said. Treating the positions held by the movements in the same way as new administrative appointments could turn an administrative dispute over the civil service into a political one, the source said. Signed in October 2020, the Juba agreement allocated the parties to the peace process specific shares of positions in state institutions and the civil service. Those arrangements have remained a sensitive issue in successive transitional governments. For the movements, the question raised by Idris’s review is whether the government is addressing a genuine administrative problem or gradually reopening the political power-sharing arrangements created by the agreement for renegotiation, the source said. The movement is paying particular attention to the timing of the decision, the source said, given that the government has appointed a number of representatives of the armed movements to executive positions in recent months, some as part of implementing the Juba agreement, the source said. “No one objects to having a state, institutions and rules governing appointments,” the source said. “But you cannot reduce all the positions that emerged from the peace process to the concept of new administrative appointments.” The movement’s position is that the first question in reviewing any post should be how it came to be occupied. An ordinary public sector position can be reviewed under civil service rules, the source said. A position that is part of a political entitlement under the peace agreement requires a different approach and must be handled through consultations with its parties. Any attempt to cancel or replace positions allocated to the signatories would risk reopening the dispute that emerged in 2025 over the formation of Idris’s government, the source said, something the movements want to avoid. Idris’s push for a government of independent technocrats was opposed by the Juba signatories, who insisted on their political entitlements under the agreement. They ultimately secured those entitlements after the TSC intervened. Reproducing the same dispute through administrative measures could make it more complicated, the source said, because, this time, it would be presented as administrative reform while fundamentally affecting the distribution of power. “Administrative reform should target administrative dysfunction, not reopen negotiations over the Juba agreement from inside the civil service,” the source said. The SLM is also concerned about a process that could unfold incrementally, with the freeze followed by reviews of individual positions and eventually their redistribution. By the time the process reaches that stage, the source said, the changes could have become an institutional reality that is difficult to reverse. For now, the SLM will watch how the directive is interpreted and implemented. Its political response will depend on the scope of the review and the decisions that follow it, the source added. However, a second source close to Idris and the source close to Burhan said that neither the prime minister’s office nor the TSC chairmanship approaches the review as an attempt to overturn the Juba agreement, but as part of a broader effort to rebuild a post-war state. The political arrangements of the peace agreement can be respected without requiring every administrative arrangement that emerged over the past several years to remain in place indefinitely, the source close to Idris said. Burhan, too, does not believe political backing automatically means shielding a position from administrative review or performance evaluation, according to the source close to him. Idris is trying to consolidate decision making into a clear chain of command, and that, in the view of the source close to Idris, is what makes this aspect of the review so sensitive for the armed movements, as it could affect the centers of influence that various parties have accumulated since the Juba agreement. A legal and constitutional source informed of the legislation governing the transitional period told Mada Masr that, from a legal perspective, the prime minister’s decision can be understood as an administrative measure governing the executive branch and civil service. But applying it to positions held by the armed movements under the Juba agreement requires distinguishing between the nature of each position and the basis on which it is held. The suspension of new appointments is legally distinct from cancelling existing appointments, the source said. Requiring institutions to submit lists of appointments made since May 19 does not necessarily mean those appointments have been cancelled. It opens a review process in which the legal basis and staffing need for each appointment can be examined. The issue becomes more complicated when a position was created through political arrangements, the source said. In such cases, it is not enough to look only at the administrative appointment decision. It is also necessary to refer to the provision that created the position or established how it should be filled, and determine whether it is an ordinary civil service post or part of a political entitlement under the peace agreement. The government’s legal position would be stronger if the review remained focused on procedural validity, staffing needs and preventing unjustified appointments, the source said. It would become more complicated if the process led to the cancellation of positions or redistribution of quotas established under the peace agreement without recourse to the relevant political or legal mechanisms. The executive is responsible for managing the civil service, but that does not mean every position within the state can necessarily be reorganized in the same way, the source stressed. An official interpretation clarifying the scope of the decision could help narrow the room for dispute, particularly over positions covered by the Juba agreement, the source said. Leaving individual institutions to interpret the directive on their own could produce inconsistent implementation and trigger political disputes. *** Military’s large-scale operation in North Kordofan paves way for decisive battle The joint force of military-allied armed movements announces its gains in North Kordofan, September 17. Photo: The joint force via Facebook. The military has made its largest push in North Kordofan since July, capturing 11 RSF positions this week and leaving the paramilitary group holding only two main positions in the state. The large-scale operation began at dawn on Thursday, a military source told Mada Masr. Forces moved west from positions captured in July, advancing along two main axes west of Gabra al-Sheikh and west of Bara, with a third, diversionary axis west of Obeid, the source said. Along the Bara axis, troops captured Sharshar and Qaa after fierce clashes, according to the source. The two areas had been among the RSF’s main bases in the region, allowing the military to push farther west. It then moved into Mamsouka and across the state line into Farsha in South Kordofan, taking both after limited fighting, the source said. Mohamed Didan, the spokesperson for the military’s Special Operations Forces in West Kordofan, said the operation involved warplanes and strategic drones, as well as dozens of mobile ground formations. The military captured dozens of RSF combat vehicles west of Bara and destroyed others, the source said. Its forces also seized ammunition depots and a warehouse containing drones. The joint force of military-allied armed movements said the RSF lost more than 120 combat vehicles, with another 60 captured in good condition. It also said forces seized weapons, ammunition and other military equipment. The RSF withdrew toward Mazroub and Sodary, the military source said. The two towns are now the RSF’s last major positions in North Kordofan, setting the stage for a battle that the source said could determine the fate of the state and have consequences for the wider western Sudan fronts. In Sodary, an activist told Mada Masr that the RSF brought in additional personnel and vehicles. It has also called up forces from Um Kadada, east of Fasher in North Darfur. The Darfuri capital has served in recent weeks as an RSF logistical hub for running operations and supplying its forces on the North Kordofan fronts, according to the activist. The military’s operation on Thursday followed 10 days of preparations, a former military officer told Mada Masr, which included sustained shelling of RSF positions and advances aimed at taking key positions including Hamra al-Waz and Gamama. The former officer said the RSF was likely to commit all available forces to stopping the advance. In his view, the military has also settled on the area where the main battle would be fought and finished preparing for a final round. *** RSF drones strike Blue Nile’s Damazin, military captures strategic position east of Kurmuk As the RSF and its allies pressed their campaign in Blue Nile toward the state capital Damazin, a swarm of RSF drones struck the city on Sunday evening. The attack came hours after the military seized a strategically important position in eastern Kurmuk. The drones hit three fuel stations, civilian sites and the Medical Corps Hospital, killing five civilians and wounding others, a medical source in Damazin told Mada Masr. Blue Nile Governor Ahmed al-Omda condemned the attack, describing it as “systematic destruction” by the RSF through attacks on service institutions and citizens’ property. The military’s Fourth Infantry Division said on Sunday that its air defenses shot down a strategic drone flying over Baling in the eastern Kurmuk axis after it entered from the direction of the Ethiopian border. The RSF and the allied Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu have been pushing toward Damazin since capturing the strategic towns of Kurmuk and Geisan near the Ethiopian border in August. They have already taken two areas in the network of positions guarding the capital, prompting the military to rush massive reinforcements into Damazin and the surrounding areas. Earlier on Sunday, the military launched a surprise operation to capture Jabal Kadam, a military source told Mada Masr. The battles inflicted losses on the RSF and secured the position for the military. The RSF attempted to retake the area the following day but suffered further losses, the source said. The military seized more than 20 combat vehicles and destroyed around five others during the operation, while also capturing weapons and ammunition, according to the source. Jabal Kadam’s strategic value lies in its location east of Kurmuk and its proximity to the Ethiopian border, the source said. Whoever holds it gains an edge in reconnaissance, monitoring the opponent’s movements and securing the border. It also serves as a foothold for future operations — part of a broader effort to retake Kurmuk and open a breach into the Geisan axis, the source added. The RSF later claimed to have retaken Jabal Kadam, but military-affiliated fighters posted videos appearing to show them inside the position. The footage also showed several destroyed RSF vehicles. In neighboring Gadarif State, further north along the Ethiopian and Eritrean borders, ground defenses shot down several suicide drones on Tuesday after they crossed from Ethiopia toward the Upper Atbara and Setit twin dams, a military field source told Mada Masr. The drones crashed in uninhabited areas, causing little damage and failing to reach the dams, the source said. Suicide drone targeting the twin dams shot down by ground defenses in Gadarif State, September 15. Photo: Sudan Tribune via X. In an interview with the privately owned Egyptian outlet Al-Shorouk, published on Sunday, military Chief of Staff Yasser al-Atta lashed out at Ethiopia when asked about its role on the eastern front. He accused it of seeking to seize fertile agricultural land in Sudanese territory along the border. A few days later, TSC Deputy Chair Malik Agar told journalists that Sudan did not want to become embroiled in a war with Ethiopia, despite what he described as a “hostile Ethiopian stance.” *** Violence breaks out between Ngok Dinka, Messiria in Abyei Heavy clashes broke out over two days at the Naam market in northern Abyei — the disputed territory bordering South Sudan and Sudan’s RSF-held West Kordofan to the north — between the area’s two main tribal groups, after a young man from one side was killed on Monday, according to two tribal members who spoke to Mada Masr. A member of the Ngok Dinka tribe said the violence began with a dispute between a Messiria man and a Nuba man, which ended with the Messiria man being stabbed to death. A Messiria source confirmed that a man from the tribe had been killed and said his body was found at the market on Monday evening, sparking fury among his relatives. According to the Ngok Dinka source, police arrested the suspected killer. Some Messiria men then tried to storm the police station to take him out of police custody and kill him, the source said. Several Ngok Dinka police officers were killed in the attempt, he added. The crisis then escalated into clashes between the Messiria and the Ngok Dinka on Tuesday, according to both sources. Fighting continued through Wednesday evening, with both sides using heavy and light weapons. The Messiria source said many of those involved were RSF-affiliated fighters who have been armed by the group for its battles against the Sudanese military. The market was burned and looted, bringing trade to a halt and leaving the area sharply polarized, the two sources said. The Messiria source put the death toll at 60, with dozens more injured. The UN Interim Security Force for Abyei, however, said in a statement on Thursday that 26 people had been killed and 82 injured. On Wednesday evening, tribal leaders from the Ngok Dinka and Messiria formed a joint committee to intervene and secure the area, according to the Messiria source. The source described Naam market as a vital lifeline for both communities and a major source of income, with cross-border trade flourishing there. The market is under RSF control, as is the rest of West Kordofan, and the group has used it to secure fuel supplies and as a staging and mobilization point for South Sudanese fighters recruited to fight alongside its forces, the source said. Abyei has long been a flashpoint between the Ngok Dinka and Messiria. Its status has remained unresolved between Sudan and South Sudan since the 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement mainly due to disagreements between the two tribes, with its security arrangements held by UNISFA. Armed elements move heavily through the area and across the border. Shemeila Mirghani Shemeila, the head of the RSF-appointed Abyei supervisory committee, presented a different account of the events in northern Abyei. In a statement, he said two people returning from Abyei hospital were attacked on Monday evening and injured to varying degrees. Later that day, a man was found stabbed to death in a neighborhood largely inhabited by Ngok Dinka, he said, enraging his relatives. Shemeila said he and the peace committee, a joint body involving tribal administration leaders and security forces, then moved to contain the situation. But a breakdown in security between Dinka and Messiria groups caused further casualties and the looting of commercial stores, before the committee, joint police forces and community committees managed to contain the violence, he added. Authorities are working to arrest and hold accountable those responsible, Shemeila said. UNISFA said on Thursday that it had stepped up engagement with community leaders to restore calm and prevent further violence. *** Gold mine collapses in West Kordofan, dozens killed Dozens of people were killed when the Zara gold mine near RSF-held Nuhud in West Kordofan collapsed on Tuesday. The Sudan Doctors Network put the death toll at 67 on Wednesday, while the RSF-led Tasis government reported 82 deaths. Both said at the time that search teams were continuing to look for people trapped under the mine. By Thursday, however, a former official in the state told Mada Masr that the search had been stopped after authorities concluded that there were no survivors beneath the rubble. The Sudan Doctors Network warned that mining sites lack basic safety and protective measures, putting workers’ lives at risk, and accused authorities of negligence. The group called on the “authorities controlling the area to assume their responsibilities for protecting civilians and mining workers, and to halt unregulated mining activities in order to prevent the recurrence of such incidents.” *** Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . The post Idris appointment freeze worries Juba signatories, drones hit Damazin and North Kordofan prepares for decisive battles, violence erupts in Abyei, Sudan returns to IGAD, but is all rosy? first appeared on Mada Masr .

items.title: Les fournitures scolaires plus chères à la veille de la rentrée 2026-2027
items.description: a quelques jours de la rentree scolaire, prevue le 1er octobre 2026 au Mali, les parents s'activent pour acheter les fournitures de leurs enfants. Mais cette annee, la facture s'annonce plus lourde. Sacs, cahiers, stylos et autres articles scolaires connaissent une hausse des prix qui pese particulierement sur les familles nombreuses. Dans les boutiques et les marches, les fournitures scolaires sont tres demandees a l'approche de la rentree. Mais pour les parents, le constat est le meme « les prix ont augmente par rapport a l'annee derniere. » Un vendeur explique que les clients commencent a affluer, mais que les prix des sacs varient fortement selon la qualite et les moyens des familles. « Les clients viennent peu a peu. Les sacs sont chers, mais chacun choisit selon ses moyens. Il y a des sacs moins chers, comme il y en a de plus chers. » Selon ce commercant, la hausse des prix est egalement liee a l'augmentation des tarifs chez les grossistes. Il donne l'exemple des sacs dont certains prix ont presque double en un an. « Les sacs qui etaient vendus a 4 000 francs CFA l'annee derniere sont aujourd'hui a 6 000 francs. Ceux qui coûtaient 6 000 francs sont desormais vendus a 11 000 francs CFA. » Cette hausse contraint ainsi certains parents a revoir leurs choix et a privilegier les fournitures les moins coûteuses. Les familles nombreuses particulierement touchees Pour les familles nombreuses, l'augmentation des prix represente une charge supplementaire. Une mere de famille temoigne de l'impact de cette hausse sur son budget. « Cette annee, le coût des fournitures scolaires a vraiment augmente par rapport a l'annee derniere. Pour mes cinq enfants, j'ai dû depenser 25 000 francs CFA. Je n'ai pas eu besoin de contracter un pret pour payer leurs fournitures. » Son temoignage illustre les difficultes auxquelles sont confrontees certaines familles pour faire face aux depenses de la rentree. Une rentree scolaire sous pression pour les parents Entre hausse du prix des fournitures scolaires, frais de scolarite et autres depenses liees a la rentree, les parents doivent adapter leur budget pour preparer leurs enfants a la reprise des cours. a quelques jours du 1er octobre, les achats se poursuivent donc dans les marches et boutiques. Pour de nombreuses familles, l'objectif reste le meme, equiper les enfants tout en maîtrisant au mieux les depenses. Lire aussi :Au Mali, les ecoles se preparent a la rentree scolaire 2026-2027 L’article Les fournitures scolaires plus chères à la veille de la rentrée 2026-2027 est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: Nigeria : les 37 détenus morts avaient du mal à respirer et ont appelé à l’aide selon les survivants
items.description: « Nous hurlions que des gens étaient en train de mourir », mais les gardiens « ne nous ont pas crus » : des survivants ont raconté vendredi les conditions dans lesquelles sont morts 37 orpailleurs présumés illégaux, entassés en détention par des paramilitaires à Minna, au centre du Nigeria. Minna, la capitale de l'État du Niger, était vendredi sous tension à la suite de ce drame et des témoignages des survivants. La police a ouvert le feu sur des manifestants, selon des témoins. Une foule en colère a bloqué une artère importante, attaqué une gare routière, une banque, des bureaux de partis politiques et des commerces privés. On ignorait dans l'immédiat si les forces de l'ordre avaient tiré des balles en caoutchouc ou des munitions réelles. Le gouvernement a imposé un couvre-feu du crépuscule à l'aube pour contenir les troubles. Un commandant de la défense civile a été suspendu. Le président Bola Tinubu a ordonné une enquête « approfondie », « urgente », « complète et transparente » sur le décès de jeudi. L'État du Niger, dont la superficie est plus de deux fois supérieure à celle de la Belgique, est riche en minéraux et abrite des milliers de mineurs artisanaux, dont la plupart sont attirés par l'espoir de trouver de l'or. Les témoignages des survivants laissant entendre que les mineurs auraient pu suffoquer dans des cellules surpeuplées ont alimenté vendredi la colère populaire. « Nous étions entassés dans la cellule, sans ventilation pour nous permettre de bien respirer », a raconté aux journalistes Dauda Shehu, un des survivants, dans un hôpital de la ville au lendemain du drame. « Tout à coup, nous nous sommes rendu compte que nous ne pouvions plus respirer et nous nous sommes tous rués pour trouver de l'air frais. Nous leur avons même lancé des appels à plusieurs reprises, nous avons frappé à la porte de la cellule, mais ils ont refusé de nous répondre », a poursuivi ce rescapé. « À plusieurs reprises, nous avons alerté que certaines personnes étaient déjà en train de mourir de suffocation, personne ne nous a répondu », a-t-il ajouté. – « Nous hurlions » – Un autre survivant, qui a demandé à rester anonyme, a expliqué qu'il s'en était sorti vivant parce qu'il se trouvait près de l'entrée de la cellule, où il pouvait mieux respirer. « Nous hurlions que des gens étaient en train de mourir », mais les gardiens « ne nous ont pas crus ». Mallam Abdullahi, qui a perdu un fils, Salim, qu'il a présenté comme le principal soutien de famille, a expliqué que ce dernier était parti de la maison trois jours plus tôt pour aller à la mine et n'était pas revenu. « Ils doivent nous dire les raisons de la mort de nos enfants. Nous voulons la justice », a déclaré le père aux journalistes. L'ONG Amnesty International a réclamé une « enquête approfondie, indépendante, impartiale, transparente et efficace » sur ce drame. « Le fait que ces personnes soient soupçonnées de pratique minière illégale ne leur retire pas leur droit à la vie, à la dignité et à un traitement humain », a souligné le chef de l'État. « Nous ne tolérons pas des décès résultant de négligence officielle, d'abus, de manquements au devoir ou de l'incapacité de responsables publics à protéger des vies placées sous leur responsabilité », a-t-il insisté. Un rapport de renseignements consulté par l'AFP estime que les morts sont dues « à la surpopulation et à une ventilation insuffisante au sein d'un centre de détention », bien que les paramilitaires ayant appréhendé ces personnes aient d'abord imputé ces décès à une maladie. Les victimes étaient détenues dans des locaux du Corps de sécurité et de défense civile du Nigeria (Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, NSCDC), un groupe paramilitaire qui collabore avec la police pour assurer la sécurité, protéger les actifs sensibles nationaux et les infrastructures. Dans cette région, la majeure partie de l'or illégalement extrait est transférée aux Émirats arabes unis, et introduite sur le marché mondial de l'or en Europe, aux États-Unis, en Asie et en Afrique du Sud, selon un rapport de 2024 de l'ONG SwissAid. Le sol de cet État est également riche en cuivre et en lithium, une ressource qui fait l'objet d'une forte demande pour le développement des batteries et véhicules électriques. AFP

items.title: Venezuela: Reform Needed for Rights Progress
items.description: Click to expand Image Petare, a low-income neighborhood on the outskirts of Caracas, Venezuela, September 17, 2026. © 2026 Human Rights Watch (Washington, DC) – Venezuela needs to take urgent measures and carry out institutional reforms to protect people’s basic rights, Human Rights Watch said today, following its first official visit to the country since 2008. Human Rights Watch visited Caracas this week and met with interim President Delcy Rodríguez, other government officials, human rights groups, members of the opposition, journalists, relatives of political prisoners, foreign diplomats, and others. Staff also visited Petare, a low-income neighborhood on the outskirts of Caracas. During its previous high-level visit, in 2008, Venezuelan authorities detained Human Rights Watch staff after they released a report and expelled them from the country. “Interim President Delcy Rodríguez has overseen a pause to the most overt forms of repression in Venezuela,” said Federico Borello, deputy executive director at Human Rights Watch. “But in this fragile political moment, these gains will only become sustainable with robust institutional reforms and the release of all political prisoners.” Rodríguez assumed office following the United States’ capture of then-President Nicolás Maduro on January 3, 2026. Since then, Venezuelan authorities have released hundreds of political prisoners, passed an amnesty law, unblocked some media websites, and announced measures to reform the judiciary. Human rights activists, opposition leaders, and journalists told Human Rights Watch that they are much freer to carry out their work. Some said they have left their hiding places after more than a year or reported for the first time on the arbitrary arrest of their loved ones. On September 18, Venezuelan authorities closed a criminal case against Carlos Correa, executive director of the free-speech organization Espacio Público. However, at least 344 political prisoners remain behind bars, according to Foro Penal, a Venezuelan human rights group, and many others remain under house arrest or are experiencing other restrictions. These include people who were detained for exercising their freedom of expression and people who have been tortured or have suffered gross due process violations. Others who were arbitrarily detained have experienced extortion from judicial officials, prosecutors, and others. Venezuelan authorities should promptly and unconditionally release all people arbitrarily detained, Human Rights Watch said. Authorities have continued, in a small number of cases, to detain critics for short periods. On September 18, Venezuelan authorities detained Javier Oropeza, a former opposition mayor who recently returned to the country. He was released a few hours later. Relatives of political prisoners said that some detainees are still being mistreated behind bars, in particular in the Rodeo I prison in Caracas. Human Rights Watch has documented torture and inhumane conditions of detention in Rodeo I. The closure of Rodeo I would send a powerful signal that the authorities intend to break with the government’s brutal legacy of abusive detention practices. Venezuelan authorities should ensure humane detention conditions for all detainees, Human Rights Watch said. They should also allow international experts, such as the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), unfettered access to all prisons and other places of detention. Venezuelan authorities should also amend or repeal laws that have enabled human rights violations, including anti-terrorism and anti-hatred legislation and rules restricting the work of human rights groups and media outlets. As part of a dialogue process with a part of the political opposition, Venezuelan authorities have announced a process to reform the Supreme Tribunal of Justice, the country’s highest court, and the Electoral Council. The destruction of judicial independence in Venezuela in the 2000s enabled widespread human rights violations and establishing an independent and impartial supreme court would be a crucial first step to a much-needed overhaul to the judicial system, Human Rights Watch said. Over the last decade, Venezuelan authorities have also barred opposition candidates from running for office. Broader patterns of repression have also made it impossible for Venezuelans to exercise their democratic rights freely in past elections. “Venezuelans deserve to participate in timely, free, and fair elections,” Borello said. “That requires urgently allowing political opponents to take part in the political process and run for office.” Venezuelan authorities should also overhaul the country’s security forces to curb their continuation of human rights violations, Human Rights Watch said. These measures should include vetting officials responsible for grave human rights violations, ensuring that intelligence agencies are not tasked with criminal investigations, dismantling clandestine detention centers, and establishing clear rules for the use of force. On September 16, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela (FFM) released a report warning that the state machinery behind repression remains firmly intact. The UN Human Rights Council should renew the mandate of the FFM for two years, Human Rights Watch said. The humanitarian situation in Venezuela remains dire, exacerbated by the earthquakes in June that killed at least 6,300 people. According to HumVenezuela, a group of organizations monitoring the humanitarian crises in the country, over 18 million people, out of a population of 28.5 million, were already unable to meet their basic needs prior to the earthquake. People in many parts of the country experience daily hours-long electricity blackouts and days-long water shortages, and many said they are increasingly impatient. Human Rights Watch has long expressed concern about the role of US economic sanctions in further deepening the humanitarian crisis in Venezuela. Since Maduro’s ouster, US engagement has focused largely on advancing the Trump administration’s economic goals, at the expense of a robust focus on reforms. “The United States should use its leverage to play a leading role in pushing for meaningful human rights change in Venezuela,” Borello said.

items.title: Programme international pour le suivi des acquis des élèves: Le Sénégal, hors classement, mais au cœur des questions
items.description: La publication de septembre 2026, de l’enquête du Programme international pour le suivi des acquis des élèves (Pisa 2025), montrant une baisse du niveau de ces derniers en mathématiques et en lecture, a suscité moult commentaires, comparaisons et classements. À l’heure de la refondation, celle-ci mérite réflexion. Le Sénégal ne participe pas au Programme international pour le suivi des acquis des élèves (Pisa). Mais son absence de ce classement ne remet pas en cause les questions de cette enquête étrangère sur son système éducatif. À l’heure de la refondation, elles méritent une discussion publique centrée sur une exigence essentielle : ce que les élèves comprennent et savent faire avec leurs connaissances. Les résultats Pisa 2025 suscitent, dans de nombreux pays, des analyses, des appréciations et des critiques de spécialistes de l’éducation et d’enseignants. Les performances observées, les méthodes et les limites de l’enquête sont discutées. Le Sénégal peut prendre part à cette réflexion sans transposer sur ses élèves des résultats qui ne les concernent pas directement. Pisa examine principalement la compréhension de l’écrit, la culture mathématique et la culture scientifique des élèves de quinze ans. Son intérêt tient à une exigence : apprécier leur capacité à mobiliser leurs acquis devant des situations qui demandent de comprendre, de raisonner et de justifier une réponse. La refondation éducative appelle aussi un débat philosophique, sociologique, culturel, anthropologique et politique sur le modèle d’école que nous souhaitons construire et sur les citoyens qu’elle doit contribuer à former. Ce débat sur les finalités de l’éducation gagne, cependant, à s’articuler à une exigence fondamentale : assurer à chaque élève la compréhension de l’écrit, la maîtrise du raisonnement mathématique et l’initiation à la démarche scientifique. Ces apprentissages constituent des points d’appui indispensables pour accéder aux savoirs, exercer son jugement et participer de manière éclairée à la vie collective. L’orientation serait donc de penser ensemble les finalités de notre école et les apprentissages fondamentaux qui permettent de les réaliser. Réfléchir sur les pratiques pédagogiques En compréhension de l’écrit, notre interrogation devrait dépasser la capacité à déchiffrer ou à restituer un passage. L’élève sait-il dégager l’idée principale d’un texte, relier plusieurs informations, comprendre ce qui demeure implicite et apprécier la solidité d’un argument ? Peut-il confronter deux documents qui présentent des versions différentes d’un même fait ? Ces capacités conditionnent également l’apprentissage des autres disciplines et l’exercice d’une citoyenneté éclairée. Pour le Sénégal, cela pose une question précise sur les langues d’enseignement. Une difficulté devant un problème mathématique ou scientifique peut provenir de la formulation de la consigne. Il faut donc distinguer ce qui relève de la compréhension linguistique de ce qui relève du raisonnement disciplinaire. L’articulation entre langues nationales et français devrait être appréciée aussi selon la capacité à faciliter la compréhension, l’explication et la progression des apprentissages. En mathématiques, savoir appliquer une formule est nécessaire. Encore faut-il reconnaître quand et pourquoi l’utiliser. Un élève peut-il comparer deux prix, calculer une proportion, interpréter un graphique ou vérifier si un résultat est plausible ? Notre enseignement doit examiner le passage entre la maîtrise des procédures et la compréhension des situations auxquelles elles répondent. En sciences, la restitution des connaissances doit s’accompagner d’un apprentissage de la démarche. L’élève sait-il formuler une hypothèse, interpréter une observation, distinguer une preuve d’une opinion et expliquer les limites d’une conclusion ? Des questions liées à l’eau, à la santé ou à l’environnement peuvent fournir des situations concrètes pour exercer ce raisonnement. L’ambition d’une société éducative prend ici un sens précis : multiplier, autour de l’école, les occasions de développer ces capacités. Les bibliothèques et les familles peuvent soutenir la lecture et la discussion des textes. Les activités quotidiennes peuvent donner du sens aux proportions, aux mesures et aux calculs. Les médias peuvent rendre accessibles les démarches scientifiques en expliquant comment une connaissance est établie et vérifiée. Cette responsabilité partagée doit renforcer des apprentissages identifiés, avec une attention particulière aux enfants disposant de moins de ressources. Le Sénégal dispose également d’évaluations du Programme d’analyse des systèmes éducatifs de la Confemen (Pasec), dont les résultats doivent nourrir ses choix. Les populations et les méthodes diffèrent de celles de Pisa : leurs éclairages doivent être croisés avec rigueur, en tenant compte de nos réalités linguistiques, sociales et scolaires. Une initiative utile serait de réunir enseignants, chercheurs et responsables éducatifs autour de trois questions : quelles difficultés de compréhension, de raisonnement mathématique et de démarche scientifique nos évaluations révèlent-elles ? Quelles pratiques pédagogiques permettent d’y répondre ? Comment vérifier les progrès, notamment chez les élèves les moins favorisés ? La presse nationale pourrait ouvrir et suivre ce débat. La refondation engage une vision de la société et de son avenir. Sa réalisation suppose que chaque enfant acquière les moyens de comprendre, de raisonner et de juger par lui-même. Être hors classement ne signifie pas être hors des questions. Par Lamine NIANG

items.title: Alerte pluie en Algérie : jusqu’à 50 mm, les régions concernées
items.description: L’automne s’installe en Algérie. Après un été particulièrement caniculaire marquée par des feux de forêt dévastateurs, les pluies automnales arrivent cette année plutôt et les températures commencent à s’adoucir. L’Office national de la météorologie (ONM) a lancé ce vendredi un nouveau BMS pluie qui concerne plusieurs wilayas du pays. Ainsi, les wilayas de Béni Abbès, Béchar, Naâma, El Bayadh, Tlemcen, Sidi Bel Abbès, Saïda, Mascara, Relizane, Tissemsilt, Tiaret, Laghouat et Djelfa sont placées en vigilance orange (niveau II) pluie du samedi à 15h00 au dimanche 20 septembre à 03h00 du matin, avec une quantité qui peut atteindre 40 mm. Alerte pluie en Algérie : des régions du Sahara concernées La deuxième alerte lancée par l’ONM touche Bordj Bou Arréridj, Sétif, Mila, Constantine, Guelma, Souk Ahras, Oum El Bouaghi, Batna, Khenchela et Tébessa. Ces wilayas sont placées en vigilance orange pluie (niveau II) demain samedi de 12h00 à 23h00. Sur ces régions, la quantité estimée varie entre « 20 et 40 mm, pouvant atteindre ou dépasser localement 50 mm. » Le BMS de l’ONM concerne aussi les wilayas du grand sud. Il s’agit d’Adrar, Bordj Badji Mokhtar, In Salah et Tamanrasset qui sont placées en vigilance orange pluie (niveau), avec une « quantité estimée 20 et 40 mm », samedi 19 septembre de 06h00 à 22h00. L’ONM annonce aussi des pluies sur les wilayas d’Adrar, Bordj Badji Mokhtar, In Salah et Tamanrasset ce vendredi 18 septembre de 15h00 à 23h00. Enfin, l’ONM alerte sur pluies dont la qualité peut atteindre 50 mm dans les wilayas de Tizi Ouzou, Béjaïa, Jijel, Skikda, Annaba, El Tarf, Bouira, Bordj Bou Arréridj, Sétif, Mila, Constantine, Guelma, Souk Ahras, Tébessa, Oum El Bouaghi, Khenchela et Batna, et ce vendredi de 14h00 à 23h00. L’article Alerte pluie en Algérie : jusqu’à 50 mm, les régions concernées est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Santé: Une campagne de collecte de don de sang au CHP-Blitta
items.description: Blitta-Gare, 18 sept. (ATOP) – La direction du Centre hospitalier préfectoral (CHP) de Blitta a organisé, le jeudi 17 septembre, sa troisième campagne de collecte de poches de sang. Cette campagne est menée en collaboration avec le Centre régional de transfusion sanguine (CRTS) de Sokodé et la Croix-Rouge Togolaise (CRT). Elle a permis de collecter des poches de sang pour répondre aux besoins transfusionnels en vue de renforcer la prise en charge des urgences médico-chirurgicales. Le directeur du CHP-Blitta, le médecin Lt-Col. Akpanahè Mahèza a souligné l’urgence de continuer à sauver des vies en assurant un stock de produits sanguins suffisant pour répondre aux besoins constants des structures de santé. « Les poches de sang collectées contribueront à résoudre le problème de pénurie de produits sanguins qui est récurrent depuis plus de trois mois dans les centres de santé », a-t-il précisé. M. Lattah Wales, donateur depuis 12 ans, a témoigné des difficultés rencontrées par des familles à la recherche de sang pour sauver des proches, et qui ont fini par les perdre par manque de sang. Il a invité les uns et les autres à donner de leur sang afin de sauver des vies. ATOP/SF/MEK/BA

items.title: Excellence académique : 60 meilleures filles au BAC II 2026 primées
items.description: Lomé, 18 sept. (ATOP) – Le ministère des Solidarités, du Genre, de la Famille et de la Protection de l’Enfance a primé, le vendredi 18 septembre à Lomé, 60 meilleures filles à l’examen du Baccalauréat deuxième partie (BAC II) toutes séries confondues. Ces lauréates de toutes les régions du pays, ont reçu chacune un ordinateur portatif et une attestation de mérite. Elles ont été entretenues sur le choix des filières porteuses afin de mieux s’orienter. Remise symbolique du prix par la ministre Cette action s’inscrit dans le projet de l’excellence académique, du leadership et de l’employabilité de la fille togolaise visant à favoriser l’émergence d’une élite féminine de qualité capable de contribuer activement au développement du pays. Elle bénéficie de l’appui du Programme des Nations unies pour le développement, de Plan international Togo et du Fonds des nations unies pour la population (UNFPA). A travers ce projet, le gouvernement entend encourager les jeunes filles à poursuivre leurs efforts dans l’excellence académique et à se préparer à devenir des citoyennes accomplies et responsables. La ministre en charge des Solidarités, Mme Moni Sankarédja-Sinandja, a souligné que l’accès équitable au savoir constitue la clé de voûte d’une société plus inclusive et plus prospère. Elle a rappelé que grâce à diverses initiatives, des progrès ont été enregistrés en termes de réduction des disparités entre filles et garçons dans le système éducatif. Mme Sankarédja-Sinandja a exhorté les lauréates à maintenir le cap de l’excellence et à faire un usage responsable des outils numériques. Le ministre délégué en charge de l’Enseignement supérieur et de la Recherche, Prof. Gado Tchangbedji, a invité les bénéficiaires à faire preuve de sérieux, d’abnégation et de persévérance pour poursuivre leur parcours. Il les a particulièrement encouragées à s’orienter vers les filières scientifiques afin de renforcer leur contribution au développement du pays. Le lot des ordinateurs offert La représentante résidente du PNUD au Togo, Binta Sanneh a estimé qu’investir dans l’éducation des femmes et des filles est un levier essentiel de promotion des chances, de réduction des inégalités et d’accélération du développement durable. Elle les a invitées à visiter le centre Unipod de Lomé, présenté comme un espace d’expérimentation et d’innovation susceptible de nourrir leur inspiration et d’élargir leurs perspectives professionnelles. La porte-parole des bénéficiaires, Guiho Akou, a rassuré de leur détermination à donner le meilleur d’elles-mêmes. Elle a invité ses jeunes sœurs à cultiver la discipline, et l’excellence pour un avenir meilleur. ATOP/BA/AO/BV
